commit_message:
curl_get_line: enhance the API

To make sure callers can properly differentiate between errors and know
cleanly when EOF happens. Updated all users and unit test 3200.

Triggered by a remark by ZeroPath

Closes #19140

findings.title: Curl_get_line loops forever on fgets() read error instead of returning
findings.message: Curl_get_line() reads a config/cache/cookie/hsts/netrc file line by line using fgets() in a 'while(1)' loop. The rewritten loop sets `*eof = feof(input);` right after the fgets() call and only breaks out of the loop (returning) when `*eof` becomes true (real EOF) or a full line terminated by '\n' has been accumulated. It never calls ferror(input) to detect a genuine I/O read error. If fgets() fails due to an I/O error (e.g. the underlying FILE* is backed by a device, pipe, or network filesystem that returns an error rather than EOF), fgets() returns NULL while feof(input) remains false. In that case `*eof` stays false, `rlen` becomes 0 (since b is NULL), so none of the three possible loop-exit conditions (dynbuf append failure, trailing newline detected, or EOF reached) are met, and the loop immediately retries fgets() on the same broken stream forever. This is a regression versus the prior implementation, which contained an explicit 'else { ... else break; }' branch that terminated the loop (returning an error) when fgets() returned NULL and no buffered data was pending. The new code dropped that fallback without adding an equivalent ferror() check, turning a transient/permanent read error on any file parsed via Curl_get_line (cookie jar, alt-svc cache, HSTS cache, netrc, config files) into an unbounded CPU-spinning infinite loop — a denial-of-service hang.
findings.suggestion: After fgets() returns NULL, explicitly check ferror(input) in addition to feof(input), and return a read-error CURLcode (e.g. CURLE_READ_ERROR) immediately so the loop cannot spin forever on a persistent I/O error.

ground_truth.root_cause: The loop exit logic in Curl_get_line only checks feof(input) (via `*eof`) to decide when to stop retrying fgets(); it never checks ferror(input), so a persistent I/O error (which makes fgets() keep returning NULL while feof() stays false) is indistinguishable from 'just keep reading' and the loop never terminates.
